an1.235:1.1: Mahāpajāpati was the Buddha’s foster-mother, sister of his birth mother Māyā. She is honored in the tradition as the first nun, the founder of the bhikkhunī order ([an8.51]()). Though mostly remembered as the Buddha’s mother ([mn142]()), her own verses deconstruct her motherhood, relating how she has previously been a “mother, a son, a father, a brother, and a grandmother” but now has transcended all such states ([thig6.6:3.1]()).
an1.236:1.1: Khemā, whose name means “sanctuary”, was praised for her teaching to King Pasenadi ([sn44.1]()). Her verses are at [thig6.3](); see [sn17.24:1.7]().
an1.237:1.1: Uppalavaṇṇā’s skill in psychic powers kept her fearless when demolishing Māra ([sn5.5]()). Her verses are at [thig11.1](), and she was as a teacher of nuns ([thig13.5:27.3](), [pli-tv-kd20:8.1.1]()). A Vinaya story shows her gratitude to the Buddha ([pli-tv-bu-vb-np5:1.1.1]()). She was a survivor of sexual assault ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj1:10.5.1]()).
an1.238:1.1: Paṭācārā’s verses recount her experience of awakening ([thig5.10]()). She is honored as a teacher by many students in the Therīgāthā ([thig5.11](), [thig5.12](), [thig6.1](), [thig7.1]()). This supports the idea that she was an expert in the Vinaya. However, she is not mentioned at all in the Vinaya Piṭaka. This shows that the Vinaya texts that we have today, which were redacted by the monks, can be quite separate from the traditions of the nuns.
an1.239:1.1: This skill is on display in [mn44](), a highly technical and insightful discussion of the Dhamma. Her verse is at [thig1.12]().
an1.240:1.1: Nandā is a common name, and it is not exactly clear who this nun is. Four “Nandā” sisters went forth: Nandā, Nandavatī, Sundarīnandā, and Thullanandā ([pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.7]()). However, Sundarīnandā is referred to simply as “Nandā” ([thig5.4:1.1](); see also [thig2.1:1.1]()). A Nandā passed away as a non-returner ([dn16:2.7.2](), [sn55.8:2.3]()).
an1.241:1.1: Her verses at [thig5.8]() speak of how she went forth in old age yet still triumphed.
an1.242:1.1: Her verses at [thig5.7]() mention her development of higher powers.
an1.243:1.1: While she features only here and in her verses ([thig5.9]()), Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā attracted a huge body of later legends. Her hair is said to have regrown curly after being forcibly plucked out as a Jain nun. She was ordained with the oldest method, “Come, Bhaddā!”. Her story is one of my personal favorites. I think she may in fact have been the first nun, and that the story of Mahāpajāpatī was grafted on later to emphasize compliance. My novella *Dreams of Bhaddā* is a fictionalized reimagining of her life.
an1.244:1.1: Bhaddā Kāpilānī is a prominent figure in the Vinaya, said to be a “learned reciter who was confident and skilled at giving teachings” ([pli-tv-bi-vb-pc33:1.3]()). Her students appear several times ([pli-tv-bi-vb-ss3](), [pli-tv-bi-vb-pc11]()–13, 18), and her skill brought her in conflict with the undeniably talented but morally compromised Thullānandā ([pli-tv-bi-vb-pc33](), 35). Her former husband was Mahākassapa, and she claims to be his spiritual equal ([thig4.1]()).
an1.245:1.1: It is said that Bhaddakaccānā was in fact the Buddha’s former wife, who in the Vinaya is called “mother of Rāhula” ([pli-tv-kd1:54.1.5]()). The late canonical Buddhavaṁsa calls her Bhaddakañcanā ([bv27:15.3]()). Her name took on many forms over the years. These days she is usually called Yasodharā, but this is not attested in early texts.
an1.246:1.1: “Skinny Gotamaī” defeats Māra at [sn5.3](), and her tragic backstory is revealed in her verses at [thig10.1]().
an1.247:1.1: While largely unknown, she might be the wife of “Sigāla’s father” at [thag1.18](). The late canonical Apadāna ([thi-ap34:16.1]()) says she was the mother of the Sigāla of [dn31]().
